en: Lokeśvara-pārājikā | Oṃ, homage to the one who accomplishes success! Dwell, O Tāraka, in the delightful [realm], united with the goddess Tārā.
Having consecrated it with the six limbs by means of the goddesses out of a desire for the welfare of men,
and then having beheld it, the destruction of the sins of those who have been seen is thereby released.
Seeing that, he was struck with wonder by the compassion arising from the torment of suffering.
When her mind was thus deeply afflicted, Tārādevī then asked: "O Lord,
ocean of compassion, please teach me, according to the prescribed ritual, the examination of the auspicious and inauspicious nature of even these signs of portents."
Lokeśvara said:
"Listen, Tārā, I shall explain the procedure for pacifying portents.
First, one should cause people who engage in sinful conduct and improper actions to be restrained."
Because of that, O Dear One, a portent arises; therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world, the rite for its pacification must be performed. O Dear One, my speech shall not be false.
It is as follows: on that day...

If death of the master occurs due to the entry of a tiger or other such creatures into a black image, a banner, or similar objects, it will happen within three years or three months; however, if one performs pacification rites—by conducting fire offerings (*homa*), great sacrifices (*mahābali*), reciting the *Pañcarakṣā*, performing the worship of the ritual vase (*kalaśa-pūjana*), giving gifts of land and gold, and providing a feast for the Saṅgha—then through that peace will be attained, and not otherwise. || 1 ||
During the day, various calamities arise through the falling of meteors and the appearance of rainbows; for their pacification, one should perform worship of the deities,
recitation, study, and sacrificial rites with contentment, and give gifts such as ten *palas* of gold, ten *maṃsas*, and ten *rasaratikās*.
Or food should be given to the Saṅgha; by that, peace will certainly be attained.

|| 2 || When a water-pot falls into a well, or when the flow of water is obstructed, one should cause the foul-smelling insects or the water emerging from the channels to be carried away by the current.
Due to various kinds of calamities, his master will face a separation from his chief kinsmen and relatives for four years;

for his pacification, one should perform the worship of the *jalajāga* (the water-born), the consecration of a well, and give a vessel of milk, a vessel of molasses, a vessel of ghee, and a vessel containing gold to a preceptor or a Brahmin.
By offering food to the Saṅgha, there is peace.

When incense and fragrance are offered in the temple, the death of the master occurs within five years, along with danger from fire and disputes; for its pacification, one should perform a sacrifice after ten days have passed.

Having performed the worship of the nine planets (navagrahapūjā) and having given gifts for ten nights, one should fashion an image [of the deity] and give it to a preceptor or a Brahmin; at night, one should offer an oblation (bali) to Kṣetrapāla and provide food for the Saṅgha; by this, peace shall be attained. 4.

There will be either a quarrel with a cat, or death, or a great conflict, or grief for a wife, and the possession by a fierce deity; peace shall come within six months. Having bathed daily at dawn, one should perform the worship of a water-pot (*kalaśa*), a fire-oblation (*homa*), and a gift in the form of an image of oneself made for the sake of the preceptor or a Brahmin.
Or one should give a communal meal to the Saṅgha; by that, there is peace.

(5) By the entry of a snake into a house, the death of the master occurs within five years or a month; or else, there is loss of wealth, fear of enemies, and destruction—peace [is attained] within seven days.
The ritual application should be performed according to the prescribed procedure: one should bathe at dawn;

one should offer oblations according to the rules of sacrifice using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of the three metals, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), the three myrobalans (*triphala*), the three sweets (*trimadhu*), and the wood of the *triṛṣaka* tree; [one should offer] seven grains of rice and thirty seeds of *śaka*; and there should be two water-pots (*kalaśa*) and thirty offerings (*bali*).

One should offer a single *aṇḍa* along with the *naivedya* and one’s own *bali*, followed by two more *naivedyas*. Having taken earth from the place where the snake entered, mixed with fish, meat, blood, curd, milk, and honey, one should deposit it at the site of the leftovers according to the procedure for the gift of the moon-disk (*candrabimba*), using a *kāśa* leaf as a vessel; this is the *Hiraṇyagarbha-daśarati-kā* rite involving milk and ghee.
Just as one should give a sacrificial fee of silver or gold to the preceptor or to a Brahmin, and provide a feast for the Saṅgha, through that there is peace.

If various creatures enter a temple, an anthill, or a dwelling, various diseases arise; there is various danger, the death of the master, or harm from others, as well as fear of fire and disputes. For its pacification, one should perform oblations for ten days, conduct a sacrifice, worship the nine planets, and give gifts of ten *ratikās* of gold and silver.
Having fashioned an image, one should give it to a preceptor or a Brahmin; at night, one should offer a bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla. One should also provide a meal for the Saṅgha;
by this, peace shall be attained.
(8) By the *Bṛhaddalīmālā-dṛṣṭa*, there is the destruction of great sorrow, great fear, exhaustion, or even the threefold separation within three years.

One should perform a peace-offering (*śāntiyajña*) for him, offer a single water-pot (*kalaśa*), and as a gift, give a vessel of molasses according to one's means; having offered the *hiraṇyagarbha* [mantra], one should present a great oblation (*mahābali*) and feed the Saṃgha; by that, there is peace.
Through bathing on the foot-joint (*pādāṅga*), there is the fear of a great disease caused by the falling of urine.

Loss of wealth occurs through *viṣṭhā*; grief for a son increases through *viṣṭhā*; and the destruction of the family occurs through disease within three years. Peace is attained through the ritual of *bali* offering. Likewise, there are thirty-two [offerings], and the food offering (*naivedya*) consists of three [measures]. A heap of rice is cooked with one [measure];
having prepared a bath with that rice-porridge (*odana*), one should worship according to the rite of the five services (*pañcopacāra*). Thereafter—

Having established [the image] in the position of a gatekeeper, one should worship it according to the rite of the five offerings; then, at the position of the fifty-two gatekeepers, one should deposit a vessel for gifts, a silver treasury-vessel, a vessel of molasses, and a golden vessel, and according to one's ability, one should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and provide a feast for the Saṅgha. || 9 ||

If there is a broken vessel— whether it be a vessel of another material, a bronze vessel, a milk vessel, or a vessel for water, liquor, meat, fish, and so forth— or if there is the death of a householder, there shall be a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for seven years,
worship of the water-jar (*kalaśa*), the giving of gold according to one's ability, and a feast. 10.
If any living being, whether in the courtyard of the temple or within the temple itself,
is seen to have met death suddenly, it portends the death of the master within four years.

One should perform a propitiatory *śānti-homa* sacrifice, having prepared a vessel of sesame seeds as a gift (*dāna*), and likewise a vessel of iron filled with honey, representing the Golden Embryo (*Hiraṇyagarbha*).
One should offer a ritual bath, gifts, and food to the Saṅgha; by that, there will be peace.

(11) On Maināka, due to the falling of umbrellas, banners, and flags, there will be great fear, fear of fire, the ruin of the kingdom, a great pestilence, and the loss of wealth, occurring within seven years or five months.
Peace shall come to him at dawn; having performed the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā* one thousand times as part of the sacrificial rite,
and having given gifts of cows, land, and gold, he should cause the fallen wood and other debris from the site of Maināka to be carried away by the river,
and he should worship the Lord of the Site according to the ritual of sacrifice.
Having performed the Mahābali rite and gone at night to satisfy the assembly of the Gaṇas, peace will prevail in the region. 12.
If a dead fish is found in a temple, the Lord does not live.
For that [calamity], the pacification consists of the gift of gold, food, and various flowers and various fruits; it arises out of season at that very moment. O Lord, death occurs;
having gone to Śāntitīrtha, one should perform the installation with the gift of silver according to one's ability, as well as food and [offerings] in the garden site.

Having placed two jars—namely, a bronze vessel filled with the three sweets and containing gold within—and having performed the gift of consecration (pratiṣṭhādāna) and the great rite of offerings (mahābalikriyā), one should have a gaṇacakra performed; by that, there is peace. 14.

From the sudden theft of gold, silver, various jewels, and so forth, the death of the owner occurs within five years. To pacify this, one should go to Śāntitīrtha and perform the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa), fire-oblations (homa), and charity; one should offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) to the deity of the site, perform the worship of the Nāgas, and provide flowers, betel, food, oil, red sandalwood, gold, and a consecrated cloth.
And one should provide a communal feast for the Saṅgha. 15.

If there is sudden, senseless chatter or falling, the death of the master will occur within three years; or else, due to the collapse of a mountain or the crying of the earth, one should perform a fire sacrifice for peace and the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā*.

One should give gifts of cows, land, gold, and the five grains on a mountain; there is peace among the mountains. If one does not see the shadow of one's own head, or that of trees, houses, temples, and so forth, death occurs at that very moment or within six months; [the remedy is] thirteen palas in a copper vessel.
One should offer a vessel filled with unbroken rice (akṣata), containing gold within, together with the ritual installation (pratiṣṭhā) and the worship of the jar (kalaśapūjana);
one should also give the Kṣatrapāla bali along with the immeasurable life maṇḍala, the sacrifice, and the installation, as well as a communal feast (gaṇacakra). Through this, there is peace. 17.

Through an abundance of various fruits, wealth, and grains such as spices, flowers, and rice, there is the ruin of a noble son; within six months, his wealth will be exhausted. For its pacification, one should go to a sacred ford (tīrtha) and perform bathing, worship with a water-pitcher, and offer a bali-oblation at the site according to one's means, as well as gifts of silver vessels and a feast. 18.
If a dead fish is found in the house, the death of its master will occur within a year;

the pacification of this is as follows: one should perform a sacrifice, establish two water-pots, offer three funeral oblations (bali) at the cremation ground, present an offering to the Kṣetrapāla, and give as a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā) a copper vessel filled with molasses, gold, silver, and food. 19.

If a householder dies due to the sudden collapse of a palace, his pacification occurs after four years; one should perform a sacrifice (*yajña*) with oblations (*juhuyāt*) of unbroken rice, barley, *khatta*, sesame, mustard, *vrīhi* rice, *vekaṅkha*, *tava*, *śamī*, *palāśa*, and *khadira* wood, along with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). One should cause this sacrifice to be performed according to this ritual procedure (*vidhi*). The mantra is: *Om Amṛtānaye*.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the mantra "svāhā.
Having placed two water-pots, one should offer the eight *kṣatrapāla* bali-offerings. Taking earth from the corner of the house where the foundation was laid, one should provide a cavity.

One should cast into the forest the gift of a vessel for molasses, an iron vessel containing gold, a vessel for ghee, and the installation of [an image]; as well as the worship of Kaumārī and the communal feast (*gaṇacakra*). (20) Alternatively, if a great pestilence and famine, along with one's own death, should occur within a year due to the malevolent gaze of the moon, sun, stars, and so forth, [the remedy is] the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā* and the worship of the ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
The gift consists of a copper vessel weighing sixteen *palas*, filled with black sesame powder and clarified butter, along with pearls; this is the *Hiraṇyagarbha* installation-gift.
Having performed the great *bali* offering and provided a feast for the Saṅgha, there is peace.
21. All [evil] is expelled from the house by its entry.
In the event of the sudden onset of a great disease or the collapse of one’s own body, the pacification of death occurs within one year, as previously described.

(22) If, due to divine intervention, a ritual pitcher suddenly falls, rubs against something, or breaks, it portends the death of the patron within one year or one month. Furthermore, there will be danger from fire, various calamities, long-lasting suffering, and the destruction of undertakings; therefore, one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*) and offer oblations.
Having performed the remedial rites and the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā* one thousand times, or alternatively, having offered a gift of gold or land,
one should perform the worship of Kaumārī, a feeding ceremony, and a rite for peace (*śānti*).
(23) If the fire dies out when establishing the sacrificial fire at the time of the *homa*, death will befall the patron (*yajamāna*).

If death occurs within seven years, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntiyajña*), worship with a ritual jar (*kalaśapūjana*), and give gifts. An installation ceremony (*pratiṣṭhā*) should be performed using a bronze vessel adorned with silver in the shape of the moon’s orb; furthermore, a communal meal for the Saṅgha must be provided. Through these means, there will be peace. At the time of worshipping the deity, if one urinates or defecates while offering a buffalo, a goat, a swan, or other precious items, the master will die.

If five elephants die within five months, there is peace through the worship of deities, giving gifts, and the offering of cows, land, gold, and food; by that, there is peace. (25) If there is the sudden death of elephants, horses, buffaloes, and so forth, the death of the master will occur within two years;
peace is attained by fashioning silver images of elephants, horses, buffaloes, and so on, and presenting them to the preceptor and the Brahmins. (26)

If there is sudden shaking of the house, or the sound of a house collapsing, or wailing, death of the master will occur within three months; in that case, one should enter the desired deity with various sounds, perform the movement of the deity, offer peace-offerings and gifts, and [worship] Hiraṇyagarbha with a bell-metal vessel filled with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).

Having performed [the rite], one should offer it according to the procedure for the great bali-offering for worship. Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should accomplish the prosperity (lakṣmī) in the home;
one should cause worship to be performed in the home with incense, lamps, and so forth, and should worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) five times or more; by that, there is peace.
|| 27 || [In the event] of the sudden falling of a snake, or by the death caused by a snake, in the courtyard of the house—

Or, if it falls and the master dies within a moment, one should perform a *śānti* sacrifice for the master. Having established two water-pots (*kalaśa*), one should offer a *bali* with the protection of the *kṣetrapāla*, along with twenty-five *naivedya* offerings, twenty-five *ravāla*, sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*), and auspicious wood (*śobhakāṣṭha*) for fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
Taking *apāmārga*, the three myrobalans (*triphala*), snake-entrance earth, and ordinary earth, one should present the *bali*. [The earth...]
One should offer a small oblation with this mantra: *oṃ sarvavighnadahanāya hūṃ svāhā*.

A copper vessel with four compartments (*catuṣpala*) filled with sesame seeds should be established as the *Hiraṇyagarbha* offering; one should wrap it [with thread] and, having performed the rite facing north, recite the *Śāntikādhyāya*.

Furthermore, one should offer into the fire one *palam* or half a *palam* of salt-filled earth from a place where a snake has fallen, or one hundred and eight [times]; by means of that, there will be peace regarding food.
[28] If a snake falls in the house, or if a killer or a corpse is seen;

If there is the falling of the door-panels of the temple of Mānāśa, the entry of various creatures, the crushing of insects and the like, the falling or breaking of the banner, or the breaking of the walls and so forth, one will not live for seven months; one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntiyajña*),
offer oblations according to the previously mentioned procedure, worship [the deities], recite the *Pañcarakṣā*, and give as a gift a copper plate filled with sesame seeds.
One should offer an oblation to Hiraṇyagarbha, perform worship, and provide food; this brings peace.
(29) If water suddenly dries up, there will be a short lifespan and loss of wealth; for peace, one should give gifts of aquatic animals, gold, and food. (30)

If, suddenly, in a temple or various palaces, a parasol, banner, vajra-bell, or water-pot falls due to the impact of a thunderbolt—or if any other object falls elsewhere—it portends great fear; within five days, there will be the danger of fire, the collapse of the kingdom, a great pestilence, and the loss of wealth. For this, pacification rites must be performed.

At dawn, one should perform the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā* along with the sacrificial rites and repeat them a thousand times; one should give gifts of cows, land, and gold. One should not cast away pieces of wood or other debris that have fallen; instead, one should offer worship and bali-oblations to the lord of the locality. At night, one should honor the *gaṇacakra*, the monks, and the preceptor; through this, peace is attained.

If various omens arise in the temple accompanied by various sounds, the Lord does not live for more than one year or even one month. For pacification, one should perform worship of the deity and fire-offerings (*homa*); one should give gold as a gift, perform the worship of Kaumārī, maintain lamps and offerings (*bali*), and provide food. 32.
Through the falling of a divine stone, or by being within the interior of a shrine (caitya),
there is death for those of the highest and other classes, as well as various portents and conflicts.
At the site of the breach, one should perform a peace rite (*śānti*) by offering oblations into the fire;

recite the *Pañcarakṣā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and give gifts such as silver vessels for worship to the nine planets and others; perform the worship of Kaumārī, and have a *gaṇacakra* feast prepared. 33.

By the falling of the head of a stūpa image or by the falling of various deities, within six months or five years, there will be the death of the lord, great fear, calamity for the kingdom, war, a great pestilence, and the loss of wealth; various diseases will break out, the death of the commander-in-chief, danger from fire, disputes, and the arising of many other such misfortunes.

One should perform a sacrifice for peace (*śāntiyajña*), recite the *Pañcarakṣā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and practice generosity. Having fasted for ten days, one should prepare ten *pala* each of gold and silver—namely, ten *kaṣa*, ten *maṃśa*, and ten *rati*—or an equivalent amount, and worship them along with a vessel made of nine parts of silver representing the [nine] planets. Alternatively, one should offer cows, land, gold, clothing, and other such items to the preceptor and the Brahmins.

One should offer a bali-oblation to the field-protectors (kṣetrapāla) from the recipient of offerings; if wood for felling or stones and the like are being carried away by a river, one should provide food for children; furthermore, at night, one should perform the great bali-rite at the site of destruction, and by means of this *gaṇacakra*, there is peace. 34.
The splendor of the land or its destruction, turmoil caused by horses and time, foul weather of various hues, and the defeat of the enemy king's forces; || 35 ||
If the new Rāhu (Apūrvarāhu) is seen and the old Rāhu (Pūrvarāhu) is not seen, there will be the ruin of the kingdom,
the loss of prosperity, famine, and affliction by enemies.
[36] When the field has been watered and the seed sown, various kinds of crops are obtained.

If [the tree] has been planted or has grown, there will be death of the master within two months; for its pacification, one should dig a pit one cubit deep at the site of the field and offer a *bali* sacrifice, or otherwise perform an oblation of meat. One should give a gift of a bell-metal vessel filled with ghee and gold according to one's means. Having offered the *bali*, a feast for the Saṅgha should be held; by that, there is peace. 37.
If a crow strikes one from behind or suddenly destroys a nest, untimely death occurs;

one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*) and offer oblations. Having gone to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one should perform the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśapūjana*), the offering of rice-balls (*sthālībali*), and the worship of the serpent (*nāgapūjana*).
One should also give a bell-metal vessel filled with ghee, along with a tail-feather from the lower part of a horse's mane.
One should give a gift consisting of a golden womb (*hiraṇyagarbha*) together with a moon disc, along with a communal feast for the Saṅgha.

(38) If [the omen] is obtained on a Tuesday (*padyasāṣā*), there is death of the master; if it is marked by a seal (*mudrikā*), there is grief for a son. Within three months, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntiyajña*) according to the rule of a thousand oblations (*sahasrāhuti*), [offering] a golden womb together with a vessel of milk and a moon disc as the gift.

And one should provide a feast for the Saṅgha. 39. If, due to the unexplained burning of a house, there is loss of wealth and grief for a son, one should perform a peace-offering sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*); or one should offer incense to a temple, a preceptor, or a Brahmin, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
40. There shall be offerings, worship, and a feast for the Saṅgha.
Regarding the rule that when a calf has been born, if it does not suckle its mother, the death of the owner will occur within two months:

one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*), go to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), perform the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśapūjana*), give gifts, and satisfy [the deities] with this [offering].
The pedestal shall measure two cubits; the fee for the golden [image] shall be ten *ratnikas*, along with food offerings.
At the time of the sword-worship, if the sword falls, the master [will not live].
One lives for four months; through trembling, there is grief for one's wife and children at that very moment.
One should cause the *śānti*, the night-oblation (*niśābali*), the ritual for the practitioner (*sādhaka*), gold, and food to be given.
(42) If a crow builds a nest in a temple, there is fear of an enemy army; if it does so in one's own house, [there is danger to the household].

If a crow builds its nest in the house in the eastern direction, there will be strife; in the southeast, fear of fire; in the south, the death of the master; in the southwest, injury from enemies; in the west, the destruction of the family; in the northwest, grief for a son; in the north, the loss of merit;
in the northeast, fear of the king and great suffering; and in the center of the house, untimely death. For these [inauspicious signs], one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śānti-yajña*).

One should perform the fire-oblation and worship two water-pots. A copper vessel for donation weighing three palas (3), filled with ghee and marked with the sign of a house fashioned in silver, should be established in the center of the mandala and offered, along with gold as a priestly fee and a cloth.

One should offer the *bali* (oblation) with the *ravāla* mantra; having prepared incense of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and mustard seeds and having assumed the state of striking, one should cause the crow’s nest to float away in the river. One should offer a small oblation into the fire, place the entire water-pot (*kalaśa*), and present the *bali* and food offering (*naivedya*) thirty-five times with the *ṣālayā* mantra.
Regarding the *sthānabali*: having invited the patron (*yajamāna*) and performed the ritual bathing, one should offer the domestic oblation (*gṛhabali*) to a crow and cast it into the forest;
this is the food for the peace (*śānti*). 43.
When a flower has been planted, another flower arises.

In the event of the death of three children, grandchildren, or others, there shall be the depletion of wealth and grain; therefore, one should perform propitiatory rites in a garden, including the worship of a water-pot (*kalaśa*), the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā*, and the offering of a bell-metal vessel filled with milk along with a gift of a moon-disk (*candrabimba*) according to the prescribed ritual, as well as the distribution of sacrificial fees and offerings. 44.

Regarding the omen of a horse or snake entering [the house]: through the entry of an iron snake, there will be the death of the householder and the destruction of his wife, sons, grandsons, and others. Within three months, one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*). One should offer the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā*, gifts, and a golden fee (*dakṣiṇā*) together with an image of the moon. Furthermore, one should perform the great offering (*mahābali*), worship of one's own deity, and a feast for the Saṅgha. 45.
O God, having seen the blood of another—which is worthy of worship through its divine resonance—for the sake of destroying all pride and aversion, it is worshipped by all the gods as before. 46.
In whose house there is the head, hands, feet, or limbs of a human being...
If the master’s death is indicated, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntiyajña*) by means of the ritual of the *Pañcarakṣā* within six months;

one should offer a golden gift together with an image of Dānacandra, distribute a great sacrificial offering (*mahābali*), and provide food and drink facing the east according to the prescribed rite. 47.
If an unprecedented bird, tree, forest-dweller, or similar creature enters a temple, a city, or the midst of a village, the death of the master will occur within three months or one year;

one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*), offer a water-pot worship (*kalaśapūjana*), and cause gifts to be given, including a copper vessel filled with ghee, gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a cloth, and food. 48.
If a *śākhoṭa* tree grows on the eastern branch [of one's house], there will be the death of the master within six months;

[however] peace is attained through that very same [remedy]. If that same [tree] has grown, one should perform the gift of a horse, or else fill a copper vessel of twelve *palas* (12) with vermilion (*raktakṣaya*) measuring twelve *ratīs* (12).
With that [vermilion], along with twelve *ratīs* of other gold for the *Hiraṇyagarbha* [mantra], the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the horse and the sacrifice (*yajña*) are performed.
There shall be gifts consisting of sacrificial fees, gold, ten *ratikās*, and food. (49) Due to a crow-omen at birth, the death of the master will occur within six months;
one should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (*śāntiyajña*) and offer as gifts a copper vessel, clarified butter, coral, and a sword.
And as for food:

|| 50 || In whosever house or temple [this occurs], the master will die within six months due to the arrival of many *bṛhataddiṇḍibha* insects; or likewise, the same result follows from the arrival of a "liberated" snake (*muktisarpa*).

In that very same way, one should perform the *śānti* sacrifice for peace. (51) Whether one has encountered a black snake, death, or the loss of life, or if there is the death of a master or the death of children and others, one should offer the *śānti* sacrifice and perform the worship of one's own deity according to the rules, as well as the recitation and study of the *Pañcarakṣā*.
One should give a cloth dyed with red lac, along with a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds and red unbroken rice (akṣata), together with gold, a pregnant cow, and a consecrated image of Rati;
and a communal feast for the Saṅgha should be provided.
(52) By the falling of a red drop in the house, the death of the master occurs within one year.

Alternatively, for the pacification of family decline: one should take earth from a place where blood has been shed and smear it [on the house]. Having prepared an offering for the *yakṣas* (1) and an offering for the site (1) using silver as the gift, one should give a land grant according to one's ability and offer gold as a priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should worship the goddess Kaumārī and provide a feast. 53.

If a snake enters the house of a man or woman, the death of the master will occur within six years; one should perform a *śānti-yajña* according to the rules, recite the *Pañcarakṣā-dhyāya*, and give ten gold pieces as a gift. 54.
One who sees his own head ablaze does not live for seven months;

he should perform a rite of pacification (*śāntiyajña*), offer oblations, worship a water-pot (*kalaśa*) with faith, perform libations (*tarpaṇa*) and give gifts, bestow gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and provide offerings (*bali*), worship, and food for ten *ratikās*. 55.

In whosever house there are elephants, horses, cows, buffaloes, or sheep—if, among these, on the body of even one of them, a branch, a head, a foot, a hand, a tail, an eye, or an ear falls into a forest or a garden due to pressure, or if these [branches] fall into the house along with the rain during the monsoon, it is a *varṣapāta* (rainfall-omen); if they fall with the *naivedya* offering, it is a *khālapāta*; and if they fall with the *arāḍā*, it is likewise.
Curd, milk, liquor, meat, blood, marrow, fish, and separately, a sword fashioned from gold and silver, together with its ritual installation.
Silver as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and food [should be given].

56. At the time of the fire-oblation (homa), if it is not filled with rice, or if it is devoid of the fragrance of the oblation and becomes odorless, or if smoke of various colors arises, the death of the sacrificer will occur within one year.
Furthermore, Śānti should perform oblations and give gifts of gold according to his capacity, as well as food.

(57) If a fish falls into someone's house, or dies there, or if it is found on a person's limb or on the ground, the death of the owner will occur within two years; [therefore, one should prepare] a single *śānti* jar filled with milk.
The installation of a silver-encased [image], the gift of unbroken gold, and the offering of food and water [are prescribed]. 58.
At a confluence, a pond, a river, a lotus-pool, wells, marshes, tanks, or a canal, death occurs instantly, at that very moment, upon seeing water of various colors.

Peace: the worship of the water-born [conch] in the house, the ritual of the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) for the pitcher (*kalaśa*), the offering at the site, the offering to Kṣetrāpāla, the worship of the Nāgas—[offering] Nāga, *uśīra*, *pārāvasa*, *priyaṅgu*, white sesame, *dūrvā* grass, white *kura* grass, rice, food offerings (*naivedya*), and a banner; and the Nāga [image] together with a hundredfold [offerings] in the water.

A copper vessel for charity, the solar disc, ghee, gold, and food constitute the installation. (59) Within five days or within five months the master will die; for pacification, there is the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśa*) in that field. Having dug a pit one *hasta* deep, one should place the offering (*bali*). There are the site-offering (*sthānabali*) and the sacred-site-offering (*tīrthabali*). [The offerings consist of] gifts and ghee-filled vessels.
For the installation of *Hiraṇyagarbha*, having consecrated the field with the waters of the water-pot, [one should sow] the five grains.
One should offer a *bali* sacrifice according to the prescribed rite, perform worship, and provide food.

(60) In whosever house or garden my form as a sugarcane plant appears, there shall be the death of the master after five days; therefore, one should give gifts for pacification, such as various garments, gold, and other sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of products of the sugarcane species.
The worship with nine flavors, the offering of the *bali*, the worship of Kaumārikā, and the meal [are prescribed].
(61) One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin, a mendicant, or a teacher, along with a meal; this is the peace (*śānti*).
(63) Thus ends the procedure for the pacification of the signs of portents.
